democratic.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
democratic.vibe: The field’s best natural communicator with younger, online audiences. High energy, high name recognition.
democratic.strength: Unmatched enthusiasm from the party’s progressive wing; took the market lead after Vance himself named her a threat. Actively touring nationally with Bernie Sanders on a "Fighting Oligarchy" tour, real organizing activity, not just online buzz.
democratic.weakness: Still says she’s undecided about running; general-election viability questioned by party strategists.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is rising.
democratic.ourTake: Our pick. She's the clearest insurgent brand in either party, and the momentum is real: rising odds, a viral head-to-head lead over Vance, right as the economic backdrop starts favoring an outsider message.
democratic.fragility: Her authenticity cuts both ways. The same unscripted style that built her following also produced a real stumble on Taiwan policy.
democratic.lane: Insurgent. The clearest outsider brand in either party.
democratic.marketPulse: -2.7 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Gavin Newsom
democratic.vibe: Polished and combative in interviews. Built a media profile sparring directly with conservative hosts.
democratic.strength: National visibility, deep donor network, executive record leading the largest state economy.
democratic.weakness: California’s cost-of-living and homelessness numbers are a ready-made attack line in swing states.
democratic.audience: National Democratic donors, media-savvy suburban voters.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is falling.
democratic.ourTake: Was the presumed favorite two months ago. That’s no longer true, and it happened fast.
democratic.fragility: An active DOJ tax investigation into him and his wife is unresolved, not just a headline that faded.
democratic.marketPulse: -0.4 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Jon Ossoff
democratic.vibe: Long the disciplined, understated one next to louder rivals. Still building a national profile even while directly denying he wants one.
democratic.strength: Raised over $25 million for his own 2026 re-election, and leads his Republican challenger by roughly 8 points in Georgia, the best number of any battleground Senate candidate in either party.
democratic.weakness: Told MS NOW directly this week that he has “zero interest” in running in 2028, and dismissed a potential ticket with Mark Kelly when asked about it by name. Says the 2026 midterms are “the whole ballgame” right now, not 2028.
democratic.audience: Swing-state moderates, small-dollar donors, Georgia’s Democratic coalition.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is rising.
democratic.ourTake: We take this denial more seriously than the earlier speculation. He has now said “zero interest” on the record, twice, unprompted about the Kelly ticket specifically. That’s a real signal, not boilerplate deflection, even if candidates in his position have reversed course before.
democratic.fragility: Has explicitly and repeatedly denied any 2028 interest this week, tying his full focus to the 2026 midterms. Worth taking at face value for now, while watching whether that holds after November.
democratic.lane: Institutional, actively distancing from the insurgent 2028 narrative built around him.
democratic.marketPulse: +0.9 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Pete Buttigieg
democratic.vibe: Widely regarded as the field’s strongest live communicator. Sharp and unflappable in hostile interviews.
democratic.strength: Led an Emerson poll of the actual field outright, ahead of both Newsom and AOC.
democratic.weakness: Never won statewide office; his market price has actually fallen even as his polling improved.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is rising.
democratic.ourTake: Buttigieg is easy to underrate in a national snapshot. He has won early states before, speaks fluent cable news and podcast, and has a plausible route through New Hampshire and Michigan.
democratic.fragility: Never won a swing-state race; thin executive record to run on nationally.
democratic.marketPulse: +0.1 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Kamala Harris
democratic.vibe: Highest name recognition in the field, but 2024 leaves a mixed record to run on.
democratic.strength: Executive-branch experience, strong standing with core Democratic base voters, still leads some head-to-head polls.
democratic.weakness: Some major donors and party figures remain skeptical of a second run after 2024.
democratic.audience: Longtime party base, especially Black voters.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: A known quantity in a party actively looking for something new. Hard to see the path back to the top.
democratic.fragility: Her entire polling lead is basically 2024 residue, name recognition more than anything else. That's historically the most brittle kind of number once actual voting starts.
democratic.marketPulse: +0.3 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Josh Shapiro
democratic.vibe: Battle-tested in the single most important swing state on the map, with limited national-stage vetting so far.
democratic.strength: Pennsylvania is the state the whole election could hinge on; strong home-state fundraising and approval.
democratic.weakness: A call for aggressive Supreme Court reform drew real criticism and dinged his market number.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: The most under-priced executive credential in the field. But that one comment shows real message-discipline risk.
democratic.fragility: A call for aggressive Supreme Court reform already showed real message-discipline risk.
democratic.marketPulse: No reliable short-term market change is available.

democratic.name: Andy Beshear
democratic.vibe: A red-state Democrat who has twice won statewide in a state Trump carried by 30 points. That’s the single hardest trick in the party right now.
democratic.strength: Proven ability to win in Trump country; chairs the Democratic Governors Association through the 2026 cycle.
democratic.weakness: Deliberately delaying any 2028 decision until his DGA term ends. Gives faster-moving rivals a head start.
democratic.audience: Rural and working-class Democrats, swing-state moderates.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: The strongest electability argument in the field on paper. Whether he actually runs is a genuinely open question.
democratic.fragility: Delaying his own decision for DGA obligations, which is ceding time to faster-moving rivals.
democratic.lane: Institutional messaging, but insurgent-coded results (wins deep Trump country).
democratic.marketPulse: -0.1 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: JB Pritzker
democratic.vibe: Self-funded billionaire governor leaning hard into anti-Trump messaging as a re-election and national strategy at once.
democratic.strength: Able to self-fund at a scale no rival can match; was on Harris’s 2024 VP shortlist.
democratic.weakness: A billionaire-governor profile cuts against the party’s populist economic message in a way rivals don’t have to answer for.
democratic.audience: Institutional Democrats, anti-Trump base voters, major party donors.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: Has the resources to run whenever he wants. Hasn’t shown voters why they’d pick him over cheaper, fresher options.
democratic.fragility: A billionaire-governor profile cuts directly against the party's own populist economic message.
democratic.marketPulse: No reliable short-term market change is available.

democratic.name: Cory Booker
democratic.vibe: A veteran of the crowded 2020 primary, re-emerging as a visible Senate floor presence against the administration.
democratic.strength: Ranked among the top candidates seen as “most electable” in a recent youth poll; deep institutional relationships.
democratic.weakness: Ran in 2020 and didn’t make it to a single vote cast. The same top-of-ticket doubts haven’t gone away.
democratic.audience: Institutional Democrats, primary voters looking for a known quantity.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: A second act is possible, but he needs a real answer for why 2028 goes differently than 2020 did.
democratic.fragility: The same top-of-ticket doubts from his 2020 flame-out remain unresolved.
democratic.marketPulse: No reliable short-term market change is available.

democratic.name: Wes Moore
democratic.vibe: A first-term governor, Army veteran, and author building a compelling personal-story campaign before he’s even run one.
democratic.strength: A rare combination of military, business, and executive credentials, plus a strong personal biography.
democratic.weakness: Only in his first term as governor. Thin executive record to campaign on nationally.
democratic.audience: Younger Democrats, voters looking for a next-generation face.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: The most talked-about first-term governor in the party. Untested at this level, but the ceiling is real.
democratic.fragility: Thin national record. Untested at this level of scrutiny.
democratic.lane: Newer to politics. Mildly insurgent by biography, institutional by temperament.
democratic.marketPulse: 0.0 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Ro Khanna
democratic.vibe: A Bay Area progressive positioning himself as the bridge between Silicon Valley and the party’s populist-economic wing.
democratic.strength: Fluent on tech and AI policy in a way almost no rival is; built a genuine online following.
democratic.weakness: Low name recognition outside political-media circles; represents one of the least politically representative districts in the country.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: The most online candidate in the field. That’s a ceiling right now as much as it’s a strength.
democratic.fragility: Low name recognition outside political-media and online-progressive circles.
democratic.marketPulse: No reliable short-term market change is available.

democratic.name: Mark Kelly
democratic.vibe: A former astronaut and Navy combat veteran whose low-drama Senate record just collided with a real national profile.
democratic.strength: Represents Arizona, a genuine swing state. A public legal fight with the Trump administration over an "illegal orders" video has raised his national visibility sharply, and he’s been raising serious money, over $1 million recently, well beyond what a senator not eyeing something bigger typically raises.
democratic.weakness: Still says no decision has been made; has explicitly deferred any real answer until after the 2026 midterms.
democratic.audience: Swing-state moderates, veterans, independents. Now with real national anti-Trump visibility layered on top.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: No longer just an "on paper" general-election profile. The fundraising and the ticket speculation are both real, current developments, not hypotheticals. Worth tracking closely, not dismissing as background noise anymore.
democratic.fragility: Says he’ll decide after the 2026 midterms, not before. Anyone reading more into the fundraising pace right now is speculating, including us.
democratic.lane: Institutional record, but an increasingly insurgent-coded profile given the direct fight with the administration.
democratic.marketPulse: -0.2 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Rahm Emanuel
democratic.vibe: Sharp-elbowed Chicago-machine veteran betting the party wants a fighter more than a fresh face.
democratic.strength: Deep Washington and foreign-policy experience as Obama’s chief of staff and Biden’s ambassador to Japan.
democratic.weakness: His combative reputation and Chicago-machine ties are exactly what a “change” message would have to explain away.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: A candidate for the moment the party decides it wants a brawler. That moment hasn’t obviously arrived.
democratic.fragility: His combative Chicago-machine reputation is exactly what a “change” message would have to explain away.
democratic.marketPulse: +0.2 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Gretchen Whitmer
democratic.vibe: Two-term governor of a genuine swing state, term-limited out of Lansing in January 2027, with the kind of resume that lands on every “real 2028 shortlist” without her ever campaigning for it.
democratic.strength: Won statewide twice in Michigan, including a comfortable 2022 re-election in a cycle that was rough for many Democrats elsewhere. Real executive record: infrastructure, abortion rights, manufacturing investment.
democratic.weakness: Has consistently declined to engage with 2028 speculation, and term-limited status means she’ll be out of statewide office for two years before the election, an unusual position for a frontrunner.
democratic.audience: Midwest swing-state Democrats, labor, suburban moderates.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: A real, credible option if the field stays fragmented into 2027, but she is not building a national campaign right now, and the field ahead of her is.
democratic.fragility: Out of statewide office for two years before the election is unusual positioning for a frontrunner, and she has shown no urgency to change that.
democratic.marketPulse: 0.0 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Stephen A. Smith
democratic.vibe: A sports-media personality with a bigger public platform than most senators, who has repeatedly floated running and has not ruled it out.
democratic.strength: Genuine name recognition and communication skill built over decades of live television. Reaches an audience most Democratic candidates structurally cannot.
democratic.weakness: Zero elected or governing experience. Tracked on real betting markets, but at negligible volume, meaning almost no one with money on the line is treating this as likely.
democratic.audience: Sports and media audiences, some Black male voters Democrats have struggled to reach through traditional channels.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
democratic.ourTake: We track him because the market does and because he keeps not ruling it out, not because we think this is likely. Worth watching if that changes.
democratic.fragility: No governing record at all is the single biggest question a real campaign would have to answer immediately.
democratic.marketPulse: 0.0 points in the last week on Polymarket.

democratic.name: Roy Cooper
democratic.vibe: A two-term governor with a moderate profile and a proven record of winning statewide in North Carolina.
democratic.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.

republican.name: JD Vance
republican.vibe: Combative, online-native style that plays well with the base; described by allies as “the closest thing to Trump.”
republican.strength: Sitting VP with the sitting president’s implicit backing; commanding lead in actual GOP primary polling, not just markets.
republican.weakness: Polarizing outside the base; his standing is partly borrowed from Trump’s, which is a risk if that shifts.
republican.audience: Core MAGA base, younger Republican voters.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is rising.
republican.ourTake: Our pick, and we're agreeing with the market this time. His fragility is real (his standing is partly borrowed from Trump), but nothing currently threatens it. Rubio's the hedge if that ever breaks.
republican.fragility: His standing is partly borrowed from Trump. That's a ceiling that isn't fully his if that support shifts.
republican.lane: Was insurgent in spirit; now institutional as the sitting VP.
republican.marketPulse: +1.8 points in the last week on Polymarket.

republican.name: Marco Rubio
republican.vibe: No longer running as the safe establishment alternative. A hardline foreign policy record, built through the Iran conflict and a public push to dismantle the ICC, is what’s actually driving his rise now.
republican.strength: Leadership through the Iran military action and an aggressive stance against the ICC have made him genuinely popular with the MAGA base, not just older primary voters. His odds have roughly doubled over the past several months on the strength of that record.
republican.weakness: Lost decisively to Trump in 2016; still an open question whether hardline credentials translate to real primary votes against a sitting VP.
republican.audience: A wider coalition than before: older, establishment-leaning Republicans, plus MAGA-base voters won over by his foreign policy record specifically.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is falling.
republican.ourTake: Still the hedge, not the pick. Vance leads by a real 11 points. But he’s no longer a distant afterthought if Vance stumbles: he’s built real, independent standing with the same base Vance is supposed to own.
republican.fragility: Already lost once to an insurgent candidate, Trump, back in 2016. The open question is whether a foreign-policy-driven surge holds up once actual voting starts.
republican.lane: Institutional record, insurgent-coded momentum right now.
republican.marketPulse: -3.9 points in the last week on Polymarket.

republican.name: Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
republican.role: Secretary of Health and Human Services
republican.vibe: A cabinet-level platform and a following that doesn’t map neatly onto either party’s usual base.
republican.strength: Built-in name recognition and an independent, health-and-wellness-driven coalition Vance can’t easily match.
republican.weakness: No history of winning a competitive Republican primary; unclear his coalition actually shows up as GOP primary voters.
republican.audience: Health-and-wellness independents, anti-establishment voters across the spectrum.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is falling.
republican.ourTake: A genuine wildcard with real name recognition, third in line behind two candidates with an actual path to the nomination.
republican.fragility: No history winning a competitive Republican primary; unclear his coalition shows up as actual GOP primary voters.
republican.lane: Genuinely insurgent. The closest thing to a wildcard in either party.
republican.marketPulse: -0.1 points in the last week on Polymarket.

republican.name: Ted Cruz
republican.vibe: A 2016 national runner-up with a national fundraising list that never really went away.
republican.strength: Existing national infrastructure and a base that remembers him fondly from his last run.
republican.weakness: Faces the same problem as everyone not named Vance: no clear lane while a sitting VP dominates the base.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
republican.ourTake: A name on the ballot more than a real threat, unless the Vance-RFK Jr. fight opens a lane nobody’s using yet.
republican.fragility: No clear lane while Vance dominates the base he'd need.
republican.lane: Was insurgent in 2016; now reads as a fixture.
republican.marketPulse: No reliable short-term market change is available.

republican.name: Ron DeSantis
republican.vibe: Widely panned for a stiff, unpersuasive interview and debate style during his 2024 run. The opposite of a natural retail politician.
republican.strength: Real executive experience, prior national campaign infrastructure, strong fundraising base.
republican.weakness: Lost badly to Trump in 2024; still working to rebuild a coalition that fractured then.
republican.audience: Conservatives wary of a Trump-family or Vance-anointed succession.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
republican.ourTake: Hasn’t shown us yet why 2028 goes any differently than 2024 did.
republican.fragility: Hasn't rebuilt the coalition that fractured after his 2024 defeat.
republican.marketPulse: +0.6 points in the last week on Polymarket.

republican.name: Nikki Haley
republican.role: Former U.S. Ambassador to the U.N.
republican.vibe: The last real primary challenger to actually take votes off Trump in 2024, now on the sidelines at a think tank while Vance and Rubio run the table.
republican.strength: Real 2024 primary infrastructure and donor relationships, proven appeal to college-educated and moderate Republicans who have never fully warmed to Trump.
republican.weakness: Has shown no public sign of gearing up again, and the anti-Trump lane she ran in barely exists inside a party now led by his own vice president.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.
republican.ourTake: A real name with a real 2024 track record, but the lane she ran in has narrowed to almost nothing under a Vance-led party.
republican.fragility: The moderate, anti-Trump lane she needs barely exists in today’s Republican Party.
republican.marketPulse: +0.1 points in the last week on Polymarket.

republican.name: Donald Trump
republican.vibe: Has spent much of 2026 teasing a third term, in speeches, on Truth Social, and with literal "Trump 2028" hats. As of this week, even he has stopped pretending otherwise.
republican.strength: None that matters here. This has been a media and messaging phenomenon, not an electoral path.
republican.weakness: The 22nd Amendment bars anyone elected twice from being elected again, and Trump has now said so himself, directly: "I’m not allowed to run. It’s too bad." House Speaker Mike Johnson separately says there is "no path" to amending it in time.
republican.audience: Supporters who enjoyed the "Trump 2028" hat and meme era. Not a real campaign audience.
republican.pulse: Not part of the active 2028 field.
republican.ourTake: We tracked this because it was a genuine, sustained storyline for most of 2026, not because we ever thought it was a live electoral possibility. Trump himself has now closed it. He has separately said he wants Vance to run.
republican.fragility: Constitutionally ineligible, and now says so himself. There is no real path here.
republican.marketPulse: -0.2 points in the last week on Polymarket.

republican.name: Brian Kemp
republican.vibe: A two-term governor with an independent political base and a record of winning Georgia without fully adopting Trump’s style.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.

republican.vibe: An experienced national campaigner with deep donor relationships and an optimistic contrast to the party’s combative wing.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.

republican.name: Glenn Youngkin
republican.vibe: A business-minded conservative who won a blue-leaning state by pairing culture-war issues with suburban presentation.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.

republican.name: Donald Trump Jr.
republican.vibe: A prominent MAGA surrogate with instant name recognition, but no governing record or declared campaign.
republican.pulse: The Bell’s combined momentum read is holding.

thirdParty.name: Tucker Carlson
thirdParty.vibe: Broke publicly with Trump over the Iran conflict and floated a 10-point platform for a new party. Keeps repeatedly denying he’ll run himself.
thirdParty.strength: An enormous built-in media audience and a real coalition of Trump-skeptical populists actively urging him to run.
thirdParty.weakness: Has ruled out running multiple times, most recently in June 2026; 50-state third-party ballot access is a brutal, expensive slog.
thirdParty.audience: Anti-interventionist populists, MAGA voters disillusioned with Trump.
thirdParty.pulse: The most-discussed “will he or won’t he” story in either race right now. Still no actual campaign.
thirdParty.ourTake: Take the denials at face value until proven otherwise. But the coalition forming around him is real regardless of what he ultimately decides.
thirdParty.fragility: Has denied running multiple times; 50-state ballot access for a new party is a brutal, expensive slog even if he changes his mind.
thirdParty.lane: The purest insurgent energy on this page. Tracked, not bet on.

thirdParty.name: Jill Stein
thirdParty.vibe: The Green Party’s most recognizable name, having run three prior presidential campaigns on an anti-war, anti-establishment platform.
thirdParty.strength: Built-in Green Party ballot infrastructure in most states from her prior runs.
thirdParty.weakness: Polled under 1% nationally in 2024, with no visible sign of a bigger coalition forming for a fourth run.
thirdParty.pulse: No new 2028-specific movement yet. Speculation rests entirely on her running pattern, not new signals.
thirdParty.ourTake: The default protest-vote option on the left if she runs again. Not a factor in who actually wins.
thirdParty.fragility: Permanently under 1%. Not a factor in who wins, only in margins if a major nominee is weak with the base.

calls.question: Which party wins the presidency?
calls.whyShort: Democrats have the better hand today. It is an edge, not a permission slip to relax.
calls.reasoning: Today gave us the clearest single data point yet: a Reuters/Ipsos poll released this morning has Trump’s approval at 33%, the lowest of his entire presidency, tying the worst point of his first term. A separate poll shows his net approval among Republicans specifically dropped 8 points in the last month alone. And for the first time in roughly a decade, Reuters/Ipsos has Democrats leading Republicans on who handles the economy better, 38% to 35%, an issue that has been a GOP strength for years. That’s the single input with the best historical track record of moving elections, and today it moved further in one direction than it has in weeks.

calls.question: Who wins the Republican nomination?
calls.whyShort: Vance owns the inheritance. Rubio is the real pressure test.
calls.reasoning: This field is now realistically about two names, not five. Vance still leads clearly at 39%, and his fragility (standing partly borrowed from Trump) hasn’t changed. But Rubio has built something real behind him: his handling of the Iran conflict and a hardline push to dismantle the ICC have made him genuinely popular with the MAGA base, not just older establishment voters, and his odds have climbed from the high teens into the high 20s over several months on the strength of that record specifically. RFK Jr., Cruz, and DeSantis are no longer where the real action is on the Republican side.

calls.question: Who wins the Democratic nomination?
calls.whyShort: AOC owns the energy. Buttigieg has the clearest route to making that call uncomfortable.
calls.reasoning: This is the least settled call on the page, and we want to show the actual tension rather than hide it. National primary polling still shows Harris leading on name recognition. Betting markets have AOC as the clear leader at 20%, up from 9% in June, a sustained climb, not a spike, backed by a viral head-to-head poll putting her ahead of Vance. Her fragility is real (an unscripted-moment stumble has already happened once). But right now she’s the only candidate who is both genuinely insurgent-coded and has real current momentum, which matters given how bad the environment looks for the incumbent party. Ossoff’s case is more complicated than it was a few days ago: he explicitly and repeatedly denied any 2028 interest this week, and his own market odds cooled slightly in response. We are taking that denial seriously rather than assuming it’s theater, which is why he is no longer our clear hedge. Newsom is closer to that role now on pure market standing. Whitmer, Kelly, and Stephen A. Smith remain real names we track, none yet building an active campaign.

issueBoard.title: The ten issues shaping the 2028 vote
issueBoard.method: Weighted voter priority, breadth, intensity, momentum, and relevance to the existing nine signals. No single poll or viral moment can set the order.

issues.title: Cost of living and the economy
issues.whyNow: Groceries, gas, wages, jobs, and whether a paycheck stretches remain the first test voters apply to the country.

issues.title: Healthcare costs
issues.whyNow: Premiums, prescription prices, and the cost of getting sick have turned healthcare into a household-budget issue.

issues.title: Trump backlash and presidential power
issues.whyNow: Trump is not background noise. His low approval and the intensity of voters organizing against him are shaping turnout, candidate choice, and the meaning of the next election.

issues.title: Housing affordability
issues.whyNow: Rent, mortgage rates, and the shortage of attainable homes keep younger and middle-income voters stuck.

issues.title: Immigration and ICE
issues.whyNow: Border control, deportations, and enforcement tactics animate both parties for sharply different reasons.

issues.title: Coalition energy and ideological fear
issues.whyNow: Democratic engagement is running hotter while parts of the right look less energized. The fight over DSA-style progressivism, socialism, and fear of communism will test whether enthusiasm expands a coalition or narrows it.

issues.title: War, alliances, and the taxpayer
issues.whyNow: Israel and Gaza, Iran, Russia and Ukraine now sit inside one larger voter question: what America is paying for abroad, whose interests drive policy, and where the limits are.

issues.title: National debt and federal spending
issues.whyNow: The gross federal debt is about $39 trillion. Interest costs and arguments over spending are turning an abstract number into a governing test for both parties.

issues.title: Rights, abortion, and culture
issues.whyNow: Abortion, LGBTQ and transgender policy, education, religion, and parental authority remain potent coalition issues even when the economy leads the ballot.

issues.title: Money and political influence
issues.whyNow: Billionaire donors and networks associated with figures such as Elon Musk, Peter Thiel, and George Soros make the ownership question impossible to ignore: who funds the candidate, and what do they expect back?
